content.comment_body: Hello, The main issue with using [product_name] for an ATS (Automatic Transfer Switch) application is the added expense of needing a battery charger and batteries to keep the controller running for logic purposes. Are there any suggestions for accomplishing ATS with [product_name] without purchasing additional hardware? Thanks, [user_name]
Hi, Could you clarify what you mean by an ATS application?
Additionally, could you explain what an AFM application is?

ATS stands for Automatic Transfer Switch—when the main power fails, the switch automatically changes the power source to the generator, based on controller outputs. AMF stands for Auto Mains Failure, essentially the same function: upon main power failure, the system switches to generator automatically.

Everyone wants a cost-effective automation solution when making a purchase, and [product_name] is one such option, depending on your specific requirements. Even with larger systems like [version_no], you still need to protect against supply voltage failures. I'm not sure why [product_name] is being mentioned negatively in this context. Could you clarify your point?

Hello, The core challenge for this type of application remains the same, regardless of which controller is used. If the controller is powered solely by the main supply, it shuts down when the main power fails. One workaround is to use a backup power source that can keep the controller alive until the generator starts and stabilizes. This could be a battery, UPS, or any device independent of the main power. Typically, a controller can buffer voltage failures briefly. For example, [product_name] can do this for about 20ms at 230V. If your generator can't power [product_name] within that timeframe, you'll need an external backup. I remember a MAS 29, years ago, which was an example of automatic power switching, but I can't find it on [company_name]'s website now. [IMAGE] Hope this helps.
Hello all, I found the manual—hopefully it will be useful.

analysis.insight_summary: Participants are discussing whether [product_name] is a practical and economical choice for Automatic Transfer Switch (ATS) and Auto Mains Failure (AMF) applications. The main concern raised is the need for battery chargers and batteries to maintain controller operation during power outages, which increases both cost and complexity. Several contributors clarify that this limitation is common across controllers, since their internal buffering only lasts for milliseconds, making a backup power source almost always necessary.
analysis.user_expectations: The user is seeking a way for the [product_name] controller to operate during short power interruptions without requiring expensive hardware. They're hoping for a straightforward, cost-effective solution for ATS or AMF that doesn't depend heavily on external components.
